awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of a Genetically Encodable Biosensor
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project is based on the translation of engineered proteins that act like tiny sensors, lighting up when they detect specific changes inside cells. These proteins can be customized to track important biological signals, such as pH levels, harmful pollutants, or disease-related molecules. Currently, industries like healthcare, waste management, and food production rely on slower methods to monitor biological changes and these slower technologies leads to delayed disease detection, inefficient processing of waste, and missed opportunities to improve product safety.  By translating this research from discovery to real-world application, this project may benefit society and the U.S. economy by creating more high-quality jobs in biotechnology and supporting healthier communities nationwide.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of a genetically encodable biosensor. This biosensor uses a conformational rheostat design with fluorescent signals to create proteins that act like tiny molecular switches that light up or change color when they detect molecular changes. This solution consists of proteins engineered to change shape and glow when they detect changes, using a flexible system that measures tiny signals at the single molecule level. This novel technology is in contrast to existing sensors that only give simple on-or-off results. The engineered proteins respond faster than current testing methods, which often require expensive equipment and take hours or even days to produce results. The benefits of this approach include instant, precise data to track molecular changes in medical tests, industrial processes, or environmental systems, improving efficiency and outcomes while offering a customizable tool that adapts to different biosensing needs.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Our NSF I-Corps project started with a question: could a new genetically encodable biosensor from UC Merced become something people in industry would use? We thought its ability to detect single molecules inside cells would make it a natural fit for diagnostics and quality control. Once we began talking with people outside the lab, we realized the picture was more complicated.

Our team included PhD student Kevin Ramirez (Entrepreneurial Lead), postdoctoral researcher Jesse Rodriguez-Reyes (Co-Technical Lead), and alumn Ameed Hashmi (Co-Technical Lead), who had previously worked in the same research lab, along with industry mentor Gehad Elhanafy. The team spoke with more than 300 people across biotechnology, pharmaceuticals and diagnostics companies, and related areas, having the highest number of in-person interviews during the I-Corps round. The emphasis on in-person conversations reflected how seriously we took customer discovery; we wanted to listen directly to the people who might one day use our technology.

Those conversations changed our understanding of what mattered most. While our biosensor can produce very detailed, single-molecule data, many potential users told us they preferred simple “yes or no” results that are fast, reliable, and easy to interpret. Just as importantly, they wanted any new detection method to work with instruments they already own—such as plate readers, flow cytometers, and standard imaging systems—rather than requiring new, specialized hardware. We also found that there was no single “universal” molecule that everyone wanted to detect. Each company had its own specific protein, peptide, or marker of interest. That made it difficult to define one flagship biosensor that would serve a broad market, and it highlighted how diverse detection needs are across the biotech industry.

These findings pushed the team to rethink both the product idea and how best to use its expertise. Our team has robust experience in protein design, engineering, expression, and production, not just biosensing. As we kept talking with customers, we began to see a stronger opportunity in biomanufacturing rather than in selling a standalone biosensor. In particular, discussions with people in biopharmaceutical and cosmetic companies revealed growing demand for more flexible, sustainable ways to produce custom proteins and peptides for their products. At the same time, conversations with stakeholders connected to waste management and industrial processes pointed us toward methane, much of which is currently burned off at landfill sites.

Bringing those pieces together led to a major pivot. Instead of focusing on a single biosensor product, we began developing a biomanufacturing platform that uses engineered yeast to turn methane into high-value proteins and peptides. This direction builds directly on our strengths in protein design and production, while addressing a clear need for cosmetic and pharmaceutical companies that depend on specialized biologics. It also creates the potential environmental benefit of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by using waste methane as a feedstock, linking scientific innovation to broader societal impact.

The project also had important outcomes for people and for the institution. The PhD student on the team applied for and secured a Graduate Student Researcher position in UC Merced’s technology transfer office, where he now uses tools and approaches learned in I-Corps—such as customer discovery, value propositions, and business model mapping—to help evaluate faculty inventions and support commercialization efforts. The postdoctoral researcher gained experience in framing technical work around real-world needs and constraints, strengthening his preparation for roles at the intersection of research and industry. Our industry mentor having now gone through the program multiple times, not only plans to continue serving as a mentor but also hopes to become an instructor in future I-Corps cohorts, helping guide new teams through the same process.

Finally, as one of the earlier I-Corps teams at UC Merced, we helped the university navigate practical questions about how to support entrepreneurial projects that include PhD students, postdocs, and alumni. Working through reimbursements, travel, and other administrative details required extra effort from campus staff and from our team, but it led to more straightforward internal processes. That experience will facilitate the participation of future I-Corps teams at UC Merced, and strengthen the university’s ability to support innovation more broadly.
